title: Construction Draw Schedules for Investors: How Draws Work
metaDescription: How construction draw schedules work on investor rehabs: tying draws to completed work, draw inspections, lien waivers, retainage and payment disputes.
h1: Construction Draw Schedules for Real Estate Investors
dek: A construction draw schedule divides a renovation budget into payments released as defined stages of work are completed and verified. A sound schedule pays for finished, inspectable work, collects lien waivers with each payment and holds back a portion until the job is fully complete.
keyTakeaways: A draw is a payment for completed work, and a draw schedule lists which work must be finished before each payment is released.
Tie draws to inspectable milestones and scope line items, never to dates or to a share of the contract alone.
Most rehab lenders reimburse completed work after an inspection, so investors and contractors must plan cash flow around the inspection cycle.
Collect lien waivers from the contractor, and where appropriate from subcontractors and suppliers, with every draw.
Retainage, a portion of each payment held until final completion, keeps everyone motivated to finish the punch list.

sections.h2: What is a construction draw schedule?
sections.body:
A construction draw schedule is a plan that divides the cost of a renovation into a series of payments, called draws, each released when a specific stage of work is complete. It answers two questions for everyone involved: what has to be finished before the next payment, and how much that payment will be.

Draws exist because neither side of a renovation wants to carry all the risk. An investor who pays a contractor everything up front risks paying for work that is never done. A contractor who is paid nothing until the end has to finance the entire job. Draws split the difference: the contractor is paid regularly as work progresses, and the investor only pays for work already in place.

In investor rehabs, draws usually involve a third party. Fix-and-flip lenders, construction lenders, renovation lenders and some private lenders hold the rehab budget and release it in draws after an inspection. Even investors paying cash benefit from the same structure, because it disciplines the project and creates a record of what was paid for.

A draw schedule is not a construction schedule. A construction schedule says when work will happen. A draw schedule says what work must be done for each payment. The two are related, but a project that falls behind its timeline should not receive a draw until the corresponding work is finished.

The best draw schedules are built from the scope of work and the estimate, so every dollar in each draw can be traced to specific line items.

sections.h2: How do construction draws work on a rehab loan?
sections.body:
Most fix-and-flip and renovation lenders fund the purchase at closing and hold the rehab budget back. The rehab money is then released in draws, typically as reimbursement for work that has already been completed.

The usual cycle looks like this:
- The investor submits a draw request listing the completed work from the approved budget or scope.
- The lender sends an inspector to the property, or accepts a photo or video inspection under its own procedures.
- The inspector confirms which items are complete and reports to the lender.
- The lender reviews the report, may check title for new liens, and approves the eligible amount.
- Funds are wired or transferred to the investor, or sometimes directly to the contractor.

The word reimbursement matters. Under many rehab loans, the investor or contractor must pay for the work first, and the lender reimburses after inspection. That means somebody has to fund each stage before the draw arrives. Investors who plan as if the lender pays up front often run short of cash in the middle of a project.

Lenders also have their own draw rules: minimum draw amounts, a maximum number of draws, inspection fees per draw, forms and photos required, and how long approval takes. Read the loan's draw procedures before signing a contract with a contractor, and write the contractor's payment terms to fit the lender's process. If the contract promises payment on a schedule the lender cannot meet, the investor ends up covering the gap.

sections.h2: How should draws be tied to completed work?
sections.body:
The core principle of a draw schedule is that each payment should match the value of work actually in place, and that the work should be something an inspector can verify.

Good draw milestones share three traits.

They are inspectable. An inspector can walk in and see whether the milestone is met. "Rough plumbing installed and passed municipal inspection" is inspectable. "Plumbing in progress" is not.

They are tied to scope lines. Each milestone lists the specific scope or estimate lines it covers, so the amount of the draw is the sum of those lines.

They are meaningful stages. Draws should line up with natural breakpoints in construction, such as rough-in inspections or completion of a room.

Things to avoid:
- Draws based on dates. Paying monthly regardless of progress can put payments ahead of work.
- Draws based only on a share of the contract. If a draw is described as a fraction of the total with no list of work, there is no way to confirm it was earned.
- Front-loaded draws. A large first payment that exceeds the value of demolition and early work leaves the investor exposed if the contractor stops.
- Draws for materials not yet installed. Some lenders and contracts allow payment for materials stored on site, but this needs clear rules and documentation.

When the scope, the estimate and the draw schedule share the same numbering, verifying a draw becomes simple: the inspector checks the listed lines, and the payment is the sum of the lines confirmed complete.

sections.h2: A sample draw schedule for a full rehab
sections.body:
Every project is different, but a typical full-house investor rehab might break into stages like these:

Draw one, demolition and site preparation:
- Interior demolition per scope, debris removed, dumpster serviced.
- Permits issued and posted.
- Any emergency repairs or moisture control complete.

Draw two, structural and rough-ins:
- Framing repairs complete.
- Rough plumbing, rough electrical and rough HVAC installed.
- Required rough-in inspections passed.

Draw three, envelope:
- Roof complete.
- Windows and exterior doors installed.
- Siding, trim and exterior repairs complete.

Draw four, insulation and drywall:
- Insulation installed and inspected where required.
- Drywall hung, taped, finished and primed.

Draw five, finishes:
- Cabinets and counters installed.
- Tile and flooring installed.
- Interior doors and trim installed.
- Interior paint complete.

Draw six, fixtures and final:
- Plumbing and electrical fixtures, appliances and hardware installed.
- Final inspections passed and permits closed.
- Punch list complete and house cleaned.

Retainage release: after final walkthrough, owner approval and receipt of final lien waivers.

Smaller cosmetic rehabs may combine stages into fewer draws. Larger or more complex projects may split them further, for example separating each trade's rough-in. The rule that matters is that each draw pays for a defined group of completed work.

Genstone Construction includes a draw schedule like this in its estimates, with draws tied to completed work and final payment after completion and client approval, so investors can see before work starts what each payment will cover.

sections.h2: What happens during a draw inspection?
sections.body:
A draw inspection is a site visit, or a remote review of photos and video, to verify that the work listed in a draw request is complete. It protects the lender and the investor, and a well-run inspection protects the contractor too, because it creates an independent record that the work was done.

Inspectors typically:
- Compare the draw request to the approved budget or scope.
- Walk each area listed in the request.
- Confirm whether each item is complete, partially complete or not started.
- Photograph the work.
- Note any concerns, such as work that appears to differ from the scope.
- Report a recommended release amount.

Draw inspectors usually verify completion, not quality. They confirm that the cabinets are installed, not whether they are installed to your standards. Quality control remains the investor's or the project manager's job. Municipal building inspections are separate again; they confirm code compliance for permitted work.

To get draws approved quickly:
- Only request items that are genuinely complete.
- Walk the property with the draw request in hand before the inspector arrives.
- Make the property accessible, with lights and power on.
- Have permit inspection results available for rough-ins.
- Provide photos if the lender accepts them.

Partially complete items are where most disputes begin. Splitting large scope items into smaller lines when the estimate is written makes it possible to pay for the finished parts without arguing about percentages.

sections.h2: Lien waivers: what they are and why every draw needs them
sections.body:
A mechanic's lien, sometimes called a construction lien, is a legal claim a contractor, subcontractor or supplier can file against a property when it has not been paid for work or materials provided. Lien laws differ by state, but in many states a subcontractor or supplier who goes unpaid by the general contractor can file a lien against the property even though the owner paid the general contractor in full.

That is why lien waivers matter. A lien waiver is a document in which a party acknowledges payment and gives up some or all of its lien rights for the work covered by that payment.

Lien waivers come in general types:
- Conditional waivers take effect only when the payment actually clears. They are used when submitting a draw request.
- Unconditional waivers take effect immediately and are given after payment is received.
- Partial or progress waivers cover a specific draw or a period of work.
- Final waivers cover all work on the project and are collected with the last payment.

Some states require specific statutory waiver forms. Your lender or title company can tell you which forms they accept.

Practical habits:
- Collect a waiver from the general contractor with every draw.
- On larger projects, collect waivers from major subcontractors and suppliers too.
- Do not release final payment and retainage without final waivers.

Lenders often check title before each draw to confirm no liens have been recorded. A clean title and a complete set of waivers make the eventual sale or refinance much simpler.

sections.h2: What is retainage, and how does it work?
sections.body:
Retainage, sometimes called a holdback, is a portion of each draw that is withheld and paid only when the entire project is complete. It is common in commercial construction and increasingly used in investor rehabs and renovation loans.

Retainage serves two purposes. It gives the contractor a strong reason to finish the last details of the job, such as the punch list, final inspections and closeout documents, which are often the hardest items to get done once most of the money has been paid. It also gives the owner a financial cushion if something is left unfinished or done incorrectly.

In general terms, retainage works like this:
- The contract states that a portion of each draw will be held back.
- The held amount accumulates through the project.
- When the project is substantially complete, the punch list is finished, final inspections are passed and final lien waivers are delivered, the retainage is released.

Some contracts reduce retainage once the project passes a midpoint. Some states regulate retainage on certain types of projects, so check the rules where you work.

Retainage must be balanced against the contractor's cash flow. On a small rehab where the contractor is already financing work between reimbursement draws, a heavy holdback can strain the relationship. The goal is enough retainage to keep closeout moving, set out clearly in the contract so there is no surprise at the end.

Agree in writing on what triggers the release: specific conditions, not a subjective sense that the job is done.

sections.h2: Common draw disputes and how to avoid them
sections.body:
Most draw disputes come from the same few situations, and almost all of them can be prevented when the schedule is set up.

Disagreement about whether work is complete. Prevent it by writing milestones that are inspectable and tied to specific scope lines, and by splitting large items into smaller ones.

Contractor cash flow gaps. When the lender reimburses after inspection, the contractor or investor must fund work in the meantime. Agree up front who funds each stage and how quickly draws will be requested and paid.

Change orders not reflected in the draw schedule. When scope changes, update the budget, the draw schedule and the lender's approved budget at the same time. Work outside the approved budget may not be eligible for a lender draw.

Front-loaded payments. If early draws pay more than early work is worth, the investor has little leverage later. Keep each draw proportional to the value of work in place.

Missing lien waivers. A draw held up for missing waivers frustrates everyone. Make waiver collection part of the draw request package.

Slow approvals. Investors who take a long time to review or sign draw requests slow the job. Agree on a turnaround.

Unclear final payment conditions. Define exactly what final completion means: punch list done, permits closed, cleaning done, waivers delivered, owner walkthrough complete.

A draw schedule is ultimately a communication tool. When everyone agrees in advance on what each payment buys, the project spends its energy on building rather than arguing.

faqs.q: How many draws should a rehab project have?
faqs.a: It depends on the size of the project and the lender's rules. A cosmetic rehab may need only a few draws, while a full gut renovation may be divided into several stages, such as demolition, rough-ins, envelope, drywall, finishes and final. Each draw should cover a meaningful group of completed, inspectable work. Check your lender's limits on the number of draws and any per-draw inspection fees before setting the schedule.

faqs.q: Should I pay a contractor up front for a renovation?
faqs.a: Large upfront payments put the owner at risk of paying for work that is never completed. A sound arrangement pays for work as it is completed and verified, through a draw schedule tied to specific scope items. Some contractors request a deposit for materials or mobilization; if you agree to one, keep it modest and tied to documented purchases. Genstone Construction, for example, does not require upfront payment and ties draws to completed work.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a conditional and unconditional lien waiver?
faqs.a: A conditional lien waiver gives up lien rights only once the specified payment is actually received, so it is safe for a contractor to sign when requesting a draw. An unconditional lien waiver gives up those rights immediately, so it should be signed only after payment has cleared. Both can be partial, covering a single draw, or final, covering the entire project. Some states require specific statutory forms.

faqs.q: Who performs draw inspections on a fix-and-flip loan?
faqs.a: The lender usually arranges the draw inspection, using its own staff, a third-party inspection company or a remote photo and video process. The inspector verifies that the work listed in the draw request is complete and reports a recommended release amount. Draw inspections confirm completion rather than quality or code compliance, so investors still need their own quality checks and the municipal building inspections required by permits.

faqs.q: What is retainage in a construction contract?
faqs.a: Retainage is a portion of each payment withheld until the project is fully complete. It gives the contractor a reason to finish the punch list, pass final inspections and deliver closeout documents, and it gives the owner a cushion if anything is left undone. The contract should state how much is held, what conditions trigger release and whether any of it is released earlier. Some states regulate retainage on certain projects.
